extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) staff, and attorneys involved in PTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings to determine whether a patent practitioner violated professional rules and what sanction is appropriate. Covers statutory/regulatory factors, ABA Standards guidance, aggravating/mitigating factors, culpability, and reinstatement considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) — Duty violated (factor 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider which duty(s) were breached (client communication, competence, candor to tribunal/disciplinary authority, etc.) and to whom the duty was owed; this is a primary factor in selecting an appropriate sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) — Mental state (factor 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess culpability level (intentional, knowing, negligent) for each instance of misconduct; higher culpability supports harsher sanctions (e.g., intentional or knowing misconduct vs. negligence).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) — Injury (factor 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner’s misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actual harms (financial loss, lost patent rights, costs to clients, procedural prejudice) and potential harms (reduced patent term, increased costs to revive applications). Note: harm need not be actual; potential injury is sufficient to justify sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) — Aggravating/mitigating factors (factor 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognized aggravating and mitigating factors (see ABA Standards lists) to increase or decrease the sanction. Consider prior discipline, motive, pattern, remorse, cooperation, inexperience, restitution, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of disciplinary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary rules are designed to protect the public, protect the integrity of the legal profession, and deter other lawyers from violating the Rules of Professional Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions are not primarily punitive but aim to protect public and professional integrity and to deter misconduct; selection of sanction should reflect these goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness to continue practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The central inquiry in sanctioning is whether the accused, from the whole of the evidence, is a fit and proper person to be permitted to continue in the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the practitioner demonstrates rehabilitation, compliance, and fitness; this assessment guides whether suspension or disbarment is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating factors (enumerated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include: (a) prior disciplinary offenses; (b) dishonest or selfish motive; (c) a pattern of misconduct; (d) multiple offenses; (e) bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding by intentionally failing to comply with rules or orders of the disciplinary agency; (f) submission of false evidence, false statements, or other deceptive practices during the disciplinary process; (g) refusal to acknowledge wrongful nature of conduct; (h) vulnerability of victim; (i) substantial experience in the practice of law; and (j) indifference to making restitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of one or more aggravating factors supports increasing the sanction; the decision should identify which aggravators are supported by the record and how they affect the sanction length/character.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating factors (enumerated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors include: (a) absence of a prior disciplinary record; (b) absence of a dishonest or selfish motive; (c) personal or emotional problems; (d) timely good faith effort to make restitution or to rectify consequences of misconduct; (e) full and free disclosure to disciplinary board or cooperative attitude toward proceedings; (f) inexperience in the practice of law; (j) delay in disciplinary proceedings; and (l) remorse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and credit mitigating factors where supported (e.g., cooperation, remorse, inexperience) and reduce the sanction accordingly; only factors actually found in the record should be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — general suspension guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Standards advise that generally the period for a suspension should be at least six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a baseline: suspensions shorter than six months are generally disfavored; adjust upward for seriousness, multiplicity, and aggravating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — suspension for neglect/diligence failures
rubrics_metrics.description: When a lawyer’s diligence in representing a client is at issue, suspension is generally appropriate when: (a) a lawyer knowingly fails to perform services for a client and causes injury or potential injury to a client, or (b) a lawyer engages in a pattern of neglect that causes injury or potential injury to a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If neglect or failure to act caused actual or potential client injury, impose suspension (length depending on extent of harm, number of clients affected, and culpability).

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — suspension for false statements/withholding material information
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspension is appropriate when a lawyer knows that false statements or documents are being submitted to a tribunal or that material information is improperly being withheld, takes no remedial action, and causes injury or potential injury to a party or the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowingly making false statements to disciplinary authorities or courts, or withholding material information, supports suspension; consider length based on effect on the proceeding and any pattern of deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement and rehabilitation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawyer who has been suspended should not be permitted to return to practice until completing a reinstatement process demonstrating rehabilitation, compliance with discipline orders, and fitness to practice; may be required to take and pass the professional responsibility examination (e.g., MPRE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions can include conditions for reinstatement such as probationary periods and passage of MPRE; these requirements are tools to ensure protection of the public prior to full reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 10.23(b)(4) — reckless indifference and deceit standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who acts with reckless indifference to whether a representation is true or false is chargeable with knowledge of its falsity; deceitful statements of half-truths or concealment of material facts shall be deemed actual fraud within the meaning of the Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this standard when evaluating whether misrepresentations or half-truths in correspondence or responses to OED constitute dishonest conduct warranting sanction; reckless indifference can be treated as knowing misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm may be potential; not necessary to show actual injury
rubrics_metrics.description: The harm from the violation need not be actual; only potential harm is sufficient to support sanctioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing injury (37 C.F.R. §11.54(b)(3)), include potential downstream effects (e.g., reduced patent term, increased revival costs) in sanction determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction should at least match most serious instance and reflect multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Standards note that they do not account for multiple charges; therefore, the sanction imposed should at least be consistent with the sanction for the most serious instance of misconduct, and may then be increased to reflect additional instances of misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start sanction baseline from most serious offense, then aggregate or increase to account for multiple victims, repeated violations, or multiple rule breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culpability must be assessed separately for each client and for OED interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: The factor of culpability — whether practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently — must be applied separately for conduct regarding each client and for communications with OED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different standards of culpability can apply across matters (e.g., intentional neglect for one client, negligence for another); sanctions should reflect the differentiated culpability and resulting harms per matter.
